title: Inducing labour when your baby is overdue
intro: Most babies are born within a couple of weeks of their due date, but some pregnancies go beyond it. As the pregnancy continues, the risk of complications gradually increases, so doctors and midwives discuss whether to wait or to start labour with medicine. The decision is made together after weighing benefits and risks.

sections.heading: What overdue means
paragraphs: A due date is an estimate. A pregnancy is generally called overdue once it passes about 40 weeks, and post-term when it passes 42 weeks. Because dates may be inaccurate, an early ultrasound helps confirm timing. Overdue pregnancy is common and most babies are healthy.

sections.heading: Risks of going further past the date
paragraphs: After the due date, the placenta may work less well, the baby may grow large, and the chance of stillbirth, though still low, rises slightly. Larger babies can make birth more difficult. Doctors therefore offer monitoring and discuss induction.

sections.heading: Monitoring while you wait
paragraphs: While waiting, you may be offered regular checks including heart tracing of the baby, ultrasound to assess amniotic fluid, and checks of your health. Pay attention to the baby's movements and contact your midwife or hospital promptly if you notice fewer or different movements.

sections.heading: Methods of induction
paragraphs: Induction usually begins with softening the cervix using medicine such as prostaglandin in the form of a gel, tablet or vaginal insert, or a balloon catheter. Waters may be broken by a midwife or doctor, and a drip of oxytocin may be used to start or strengthen contractions.

Induction can take a day or longer, and contractions can feel stronger or more frequent than in natural labour. Pain relief options, including epidural, are discussed beforehand. Inductions sometimes lead to assisted delivery or Caesarean section, and the baby's heartbeat is monitored.

sections.heading: Making your choice
paragraphs: You can accept induction, choose to wait with close monitoring, or discuss alternatives such as membrane sweeping, which may encourage labour to begin. Think about your own health, your baby's condition, and your preferences for the birth. You have the right to ask questions and to decide.

examples.title: Discussing timing
examples.text: Imagine you are a week past your due date and offered an induction. You could ask what the risk of waiting is for your situation, how monitoring would work, and what each method of induction involves.

examples.title: Getting ready
examples.text: Suppose your induction is booked. You might pack a bag, plan childcare, ask about pain relief and decide who will accompany you.

questions: What are the benefits and risks of induction compared with waiting in my situation?
Which method would be used, and how long might it take?
What will happen if induction does not start labour?
